694.title: How to keep reading
694.hook: you've read Genesis, Exodus, Psalms, the prophets, two gospels and three letters
694.howItsDone: Christians read the Bible in many ways: through a church lectionary, a yearly reading plan, or slow prayerful reading such as lectio divina, often in a small group or alongside their congregation's Sunday readings.

segments.voice: Yesterday, two short notes from the elder, and your line was face to face. Who did you see in person instead of on a screen? Day six hundred ninety-four.

A lesson a day opens one page. But the book on the shelf is thick, and some evenings you may want more than a lesson gives. Maybe a psalm before bed. Maybe the rest of a story the lesson only touched. This year the lessons have walked from a garden in Genesis to a few short letters near the back of the book, and tomorrow they keep walking. Today, though, isn't about one passage. It's about the reading you might do on your own, alongside the lessons, and how Christians have kept this book open, alone and together.

Start with what kind of book it is. It isn't really one book; it's a library, written in Hebrew, Aramaic and Greek: poems, laws, letters, stories, songs and visions. Churches even shelve it a little differently: Catholic and Orthodox Bibles hold books that Protestant Bibles usually leave out or print in a separate section. So the first tip is a library's tip: you don't have to read the shelves in order. Christians have found many ways in. Some follow a lectionary, a set of readings for each day or each Sunday, so a whole congregation hears the same passage the same week. Catholic, Orthodox, Anglican and Lutheran churches, among others, use one. Some follow a reading plan, a few chapters a day, through the whole Bible in a year. And some read very slowly. The Rule of Saint Benedict sets aside hours for monks to give to lectio divina, holy reading. As it's often taught today, that means a short passage, read again and again, until one word catches and stays. The second tip: read with someone. The letter to the Colossians asks to be read aloud in church, and then passed on to be read in the next town. A friend, a group, a church study, even one person who texts you a verse each morning keeps the book open. And the third: some readers find it keeps surprising them. A psalm read young can sound different years later. Here is a verse from Psalm 119, in the King James Bible: "Thy word is a lamp unto my feet, and a light unto my path." A lamp for your feet, not a floodlight for the whole road. Enough light for the next step, and then the next.
screen: `A LECTIONARY, A PLAN, A SLOW PAGE.`
then, large: `A LIGHT UNTO MY PATH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: choose your next book. Settle, and breathe. Think back over the year. Which part pulled at you? If you loved the stories, you might try Acts, the story of the first churches, or Ruth, a short story you can read in one sitting. If the Psalms spoke to you, you could keep one psalm a day. If you want more of Jesus, Mark is short and fast, and Matthew holds the Sermon on the Mount. Don't pick the hardest one. Pick the one you'll actually open. Then picture where and when: a chair, a time of day, a lamp. If you pray, you can ask for an open heart as you read. The bell holds the time.
How to keep reading. A library, not a single book: a lectionary, a plan or one slow page, ideally with someone beside you.
Your line: the book keeps opening. Today, read the first few verses of the book you chose, and stop where something catches. Day six hundred ninety-four.

695.title: Christmas: the Word again (John 1:14)
695.hook: at Christmas, churches read John's prologue: the Word became flesh
695.tomorrow: Year two close: the book in your hands
695.howItsDone: In Catholic, Anglican and many Protestant churches, John 1:1–14 is read on Christmas Day and often as the last lesson at services of lessons and carols; Orthodox churches read Matthew's account of the Magi at the Nativity and John's prologue at Easter.

segments.voice: Yesterday, how to keep reading, and your line was the book keeps opening. Which book did you choose, and what caught you? Day six hundred ninety-five.

Two Christmas readings, and they could hardly be more different. One is from Luke: shepherds, a manger, angels over the fields at night. The other is from John, and it has no manger at all. No shepherds, no star, no inn. It starts before time: in the beginning was the Word. In many churches, Luke's story is read at night, and John's opening is read on Christmas morning, or as the last reading at a candlelit service of lessons and carols. You read both Gospels this year. Today we come back to one verse in John, the one that makes it a Christmas text.

John's Gospel opens the way Genesis does. In the King James Bible: "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God." The Word, in Greek the logos: speech, reason, the meaning behind everything. Then: "And the light shineth in darkness; and the darkness comprehended it not." And then the verse the whole passage leans toward, verse fourteen: "And the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us, (and we beheld his glory, the glory as of the only begotten of the Father,) full of grace and truth." You met this verse in the autumn, through its tent: dwelt, in Greek, is pitched his tent. At Christmas, churches lean on the other word. Flesh. In Greek, sarx, the plain word for the stuff of bodies. John could have said the Word appeared, or visited. He says it became flesh. Not an idea, not a voice from the sky. At Christmas that flesh is a baby: someone who has to be fed, changed, carried and kept warm. Christians say the Word that was there in the beginning started out that small. Churches keep the day a little differently. Many celebrate on December twenty-fifth; many Orthodox churches that follow the older Julian calendar celebrate on what is now January seventh. Catholic, Anglican and many Protestant churches read this prologue on Christmas Day. In the Orthodox liturgy for the Nativity, the Gospel is Matthew's story of the Magi, and John's prologue is read at Easter instead. Same verse, same wonder, different places in the year. Luke tells you where he was born. John tells you who was born.
screen: `A BABY WHO HAS TO BE FED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: read John 1:1–14 by a light. If you can, turn the room lights down and light one lamp or candle, safely. Settle, and breathe. Open to the first chapter of John and read the first fourteen verses slowly, out loud if you like. When you reach the light shining in the darkness, look at the flame for one breath. When you reach the Word made flesh, think of one ordinary body you love: a hand, a face, a child asleep. Christians say God came that close. If you pray, you can read verse fourteen once more, slowly, as your prayer. The bell holds the time.
Christmas. The feast of the birth of Jesus, when John's Gospel says the Word was made flesh and pitched his tent among us.
Your line: he dwelt among us. Today, look for the holy in something ordinary and close by: a meal, a voice, a face across the table. Day six hundred ninety-five.

696.title: Year two close: the book in your hands
696.hook: a library you've walked through, from the garden to the shore at breakfast
696.howItsDone: Some Christians keep a favorite verse close, memorized, written in a Bible's margin or posted at home, and churches sometimes mark the end of a season of reading with a time of looking back and giving thanks.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Christmas and the Word made flesh, and your line was he dwelt among us. Where did you find the holy in something ordinary? Day six hundred ninety-six.

This year began in a garden, where God walked in the cool of the day. Then came a desert crossed by a whole people. A room full of songs, some joyful, some furious. Prophets shouting in the street. Then Luke and John, all the way to a charcoal fire on a beach at dawn where, in John's telling, the risen Jesus cooked breakfast for his friends. And lately, a few letters left on the table. Today is the last day of year two. Before it closes, one look back, and one verse to take with you.
screen: `A GARDEN, A DESERT, A ROOM OF SONGS.`

segments.voice: Year two had seven parts. Genesis: beginnings, a garden, a flood, a family that kept going wrong and kept being carried. Exodus: slaves, a sea, manna, a mountain, a golden calf, and long years in the wilderness. The Psalms and the wisdom books: prayers for every mood, and wisdom that knows life is short and good. The prophets: a burning coal, a potter, dry bones, a sulking prophet, a king on a donkey. Luke, read through: outsiders, meals and mercy. John, read through: the Word, the signs, the bread and the light and the good shepherd, and that breakfast on the shore. And three letters of joy, faith and love: Philippians, James and First John, with the elder's two short notes. Now the verse for today. Near the end of Deuteronomy, Moses gives his last speeches before the people cross into the land without him. He tells them the commandment isn't hidden away. It isn't up in heaven, where someone would have to climb and fetch it. It isn't across the sea, where someone would have to sail out and bring it back. In the King James Bible: "But the word is very nigh unto thee, in thy mouth, and in thy heart, that thou mayest do it." Very nigh. Near. The Hebrew word is karov: close by, within reach. Centuries later, Paul quoted this same line in his letter to the Romans: "The word is nigh thee, even in thy mouth, and in thy heart." The verse is read in Jewish and Christian tradition, each in its own way. But the picture is shared: the word isn't a far-off mountain only experts can climb. It's meant to be near enough to say, and to keep. After a year of reading, the book itself is in your hands.
screen: `NOT IN HEAVEN, NOT ACROSS THE SEA.`
then, large: `THE WORD IS VERY NIGH UNTO THEE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: write the one verse you'll keep. Settle, and breathe. Let the year go past: the garden, the desert, the songs, the prophets, the roads of Luke, the shore in John, the letters. Which verse stayed? Maybe the Lord is my shepherd. Maybe a line from a prophet, or no fear in love, or something small nobody else would pick. Don't choose the most famous one. Choose the one that's already near you, the one you catch yourself saying. After the bell, write it down by hand. If you pray, you can give thanks for a year of reading. The bell holds the time.
Year two close. A year of the book read in order, from the garden to the shore, and a word that stays near.

Your line: the word is near you. Today, put your verse where your hand will find it: a pocket, a wallet, a phone case. Tomorrow, year three begins with Joshua and the long story of Israel. Day six hundred ninety-six.

697.title: Be strong and courageous (Joshua 1:1–9)
697.hook: Moses is gone, and Joshua is told three times: be strong, don't be afraid
697.howItsDone: Some Christians turn to Joshua 1:9 before a hard new beginning, such as a move, a new job or an exam, and some memorize it or keep it written where they will see it.

segments.voice: Yesterday closed year two, and your line was the word is near you. Did your hand find the verse you kept? Year three starts now. Day six hundred ninety-seven.

"Moses my servant is dead." That is how God's first words to Joshua in this book begin. No easing in. Moses was the one who stood before Pharaoh, who went up the mountain, who spoke with God on everyone's behalf. Joshua was his assistant; the opening verse calls him "Moses' minister." Now the people are camped beside the Jordan River, the land is on the far side, and the one person who always seemed to know what came next is gone. The very same sentence moves on: "now therefore arise, go over this Jordan." And before Joshua takes a single step, God tells him the same thing again, and then again. Today's words are what he hears.

Year three is the long story: Israel after the wilderness, from Joshua all the way to the return from exile. It opens with a handover. In the first nine verses of Joshua, God tells Joshua three times to be strong. In the King James Bible, verse six: "Be strong and of a good courage." Verse seven pushes further: "Only be thou strong and very courageous." Verse nine turns it into a question: "Have not I commanded thee? Be strong and of a good courage; be not afraid, neither be thou dismayed: for the LORD thy God is with thee whithersoever thou goest." Some readers notice that people rarely need to be told three times to be brave unless something in them is shaking. The text never says what Joshua felt. It only gives him the words. Now look at where the courage is supposed to come from. It isn't a speech about Joshua's gifts. Each time, the reason points away from him. Verse five: "as I was with Moses, so I will be with thee: I will not fail thee, nor forsake thee." Verse nine: God is with him wherever he goes. The strength rests on company, not on confidence. And there's a surprise tucked in the middle. Verse eight ties the whole command to a book: "This book of the law shall not depart out of thy mouth; but thou shalt meditate therein day and night." The first thing asked of a new leader about to cross a river is to keep reading. Some Christians turn to this chapter at new starts. The line this lesson carries out of it is the quiet one in verse five: I will not fail thee.
screen: then, large: `I WILL NOT FAIL THEE, NOR FORSAKE THEE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: do one thing that needs courage. Settle, and breathe. Let one small, real thing come to mind that you've been putting off because it unsettles you a little: a phone call, an apology, a question you haven't asked, an appointment, a first page. Don't solve it. Just name it, and pick the very first step, small enough to take today. Then sit with the words Joshua heard: be strong, be not afraid. If you pray, you can hold that one thing up and rest on the promise, I will not fail thee. If you don't, simply breathe with it until the bell. The bell holds the time.
Be strong and courageous. What God tells Joshua, again and again, as Moses' work passes into his hands: courage resting on company, not on confidence.
Your line: I will not fail you. Today, take the first step on the thing you named, before lunch if you can. Tomorrow, a woman on the wall of Jericho. Day six hundred ninety-seven.

698.title: Rahab's scarlet cord (Joshua 2)
698.hook: a woman on the city wall hides two spies and hangs a red cord from her window
698.howItsDone: Christians meet Rahab in sermons on Hebrews 11 and on welcoming outsiders, and some churches teach the scarlet cord as a sign of rescue.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Joshua heard be strong, again and again, and your line was I will not fail you. What first step did you take? Day six hundred ninety-eight.

A red line hangs from a window in a city wall. Behind it, a woman is waiting. A little earlier, Joshua sent two men across the river to spy out Jericho, and in the King James words they "came into an harlot's house, named Rahab, and lodged there." The Bible doesn't tidy up who she is. Her house is built into the town wall itself. Word reaches the king of Jericho that Israelite spies are inside, and his men come to her door. Rahab has already taken the spies up to her roof and hidden them under stalks of flax she had laid out on the roof. She tells the king's men the strangers left at dark, and if they hurry, they'll catch them. Today: why she did it, and what that red line means.
screen: `TWO SPIES, ONE HOUSE IN THE WALL.`

segments.voice: Rahab gives her reason in her own words, and it's a confession from an outsider. She tells the spies her city has heard what Israel's God has done, and their hearts have melted. Then, in the King James Bible: "for the LORD your God, he is God in heaven above, and in earth beneath." Those words echo, almost exactly, what Moses tells Israel in Deuteronomy. A Canaanite woman, inside a city about to fall, speaks Israel's own creed back to Israel's spies. Then she asks for one thing. The Hebrew word is chesed: loyal kindness. I showed you kindness; show kindness to my father's house. Spare my parents, my brothers, my sisters. The spies agree and give her a sign. She lets them down from her window by a cord, and they tell her: "thou shalt bind this line of scarlet thread in the window which thou didst let us down by." Everyone inside that house will be safe. Then comes the chapter's quiet detail. As soon as the spies are gone: "And she bound the scarlet line in the window." She doesn't wait for the army. She hangs the sign of the promise while nothing has happened yet, and lives under it. Readers have found more than one thing in that thread. Some Christian readers see it as a picture of rescue through blood, like the blood on the doorposts at Passover. Others simply see a woman staking her family on a promise from strangers. And the story doesn't end with Jericho. The letter to the Hebrews names her: "By faith the harlot Rahab perished not with them that believed not, when she had received the spies with peace." James praises what she did. Matthew's family line of Jesus includes a Rachab, traditionally taken to be her. The woman on the wall ends up inside the story.
screen: `SHE TIES IT BEFORE THE ARMY COMES.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: help someone at a risk to yourself. Settle, and breathe. Rahab's risk was her life. Yours can be far smaller: speaking up for someone who's being talked about, sitting with the person nobody else sits with, giving time you'd rather keep, saying out loud that you agree with the unpopular one. Let one person come to mind who could use someone on their side. Ask what it would cost you to help, and whether you can pay it today. If you pray, you can hold that person up by name. If you don't, simply keep them in mind and breathe. The bell holds the time.
Rahab's scarlet cord. The red line she tied in her window: the sign of a promise, hung before anyone came to keep it.
Your line: the cord in the window. Today, do the helpful thing you named, even if it costs you a little, and do it before you're sure it's safe. Day six hundred ninety-eight.

699.title: Twelve stones (Joshua 3–4)
699.hook: the Jordan parts, and they pile stones so their children will ask what they mean
699.howItsDone: Some Christians keep a stone, a cross or another small object as a reminder of a time they believe God carried them through, and some families make a habit of telling those stories to their children.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Rahab tied a red line in her window, and your line was the cord in the window. Whom did you help, and what did it cost you? Day six hundred ninety-nine.

"What mean ye by these stones?" That question is the reason for today's whole story, and nobody has asked it yet. The people are on the bank of the Jordan, and the river is not low. The text says the Jordan "overfloweth all his banks all the time of harvest." Joshua tells the priests to carry the ark of the covenant straight to the edge. Not to wait for the water to move. To walk in. Their feet touch the water, and upstream the river stops and rises up in a heap. The priests stand in the middle of the riverbed on dry ground while all the people pass over. Then Joshua gives an odd order before anyone moves on: go back in, and pick up some rocks.

One man from each of the twelve tribes is to take a stone on his shoulder, from the very place where the priests' feet stood. Before anyone lifts one, Joshua tells them why, in the King James Bible: "That this may be a sign among you, that when your children ask their fathers in time to come, saying, What mean ye by these stones?" And the answer is a story: the waters of the Jordan were cut off before the ark. They carry the stones to Gilgal, where the people camp that night, and Joshua sets them up there. Look at the design. These stones don't explain themselves. The text mentions no writing on them. They're a heap of river rocks in a strange place, and that's the point. They're built to make a child stop and ask. A memorial that only works when someone asks a question, and someone else tells the story. The chapter says it a second time near the end, in case anyone missed it: "Then ye shall let your children know, saying, Israel came over this Jordan on dry land." There's a stranger detail in between. Verse nine says Joshua also set up twelve stones in the middle of the river, where the priests had stood, "and they are there unto this day." One pile on the bank where anyone can see it. Another in the riverbed, under the water once it flows again. The text never explains the second pile. Some readers hear in it a reminder that part of what carries a person stays out of sight. And the last verse of the chapter widens the circle. It was done so "that all the people of the earth might know the hand of the LORD." The stones were for Israel's children, and for everybody else watching.
screen: `A STONE FROM WHERE THE PRIESTS STOOD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: keep one object that reminds you of grace. Settle, and breathe. Look around. Is there something in reach that marks a time you were carried through: a ring, a key, a card, a photo, a stone from a beach, a hospital bracelet, a chipped mug? If nothing's in reach, let one come to mind. Hold it, or picture it. Ask what story it would tell if a child picked it up and said, what's this? Let yourself remember the river you crossed. If you pray, you can give thanks for it. If you don't, simply hold the memory and breathe. The bell holds the time.
Twelve stones. River rocks set up at Gilgal, so that children would ask what they mean and hear the story.
Your line: what do these stones mean? Today, put your object where you'll see it, and if anyone asks about it, tell them the story. Day six hundred ninety-nine.

700.title: The walls of Jericho (Joshua 6)
700.hook: seven days of marching, trumpets, a shout; readers across traditions wrestle honestly with the violence of the conquest stories
700.tomorrow: As for me and my house
700.howItsDone: Christians read Joshua 6 in different ways, as ancient history, as a picture of spiritual struggle, or beside texts that push against it, and some Bible study groups take time to discuss its violence openly.

segments.voice: Yesterday, twelve stones from the riverbed, and your line was what do these stones mean? Did anyone ask about your object? Day seven hundred.

"Ye shall not shout, nor make any noise with your voice, neither shall any word proceed out of your mouth." That is Joshua's order to an army. Not sharpen your swords. Be quiet. Jericho is shut up tight: nobody going out, nobody coming in. Once a day for six days, Israel walks around the city: armed men in front, then seven priests blowing trumpets of rams' horns, then the ark, then the rest, and not one word from the people. On the seventh day they circle it seven times. The priests blow, Joshua says shout, the people shout with a great shout, and the text says the wall fell down flat. The chapter doesn't stop when the wall falls. Today is about what comes after, too.

Here is the verse after the shout, in the King James Bible: "And they utterly destroyed all that was in the city, both man and woman, young and old, and ox, and sheep, and ass, with the edge of the sword." Read slowly, it's hard to hear. The Hebrew word behind it is cherem: something devoted to God and taken out of ordinary use, which in war meant destruction. The King James renders it accursed. Jews and Christians have both lived with this chapter, and readers do not handle it the same way. Some read it as history: a brutal practice of the ancient world, told plainly, and not a pattern for anyone today. Some Christian teachers have read the battles as a picture of an inner war against greed, pride and fear. Some read the conquest beside the parts of the Bible that push against it, and the text itself pushes. In this very chapter, the one household spared is a Canaanite household: Rahab's, under the red line. And just before the march, Joshua meets a man with a drawn sword and asks, "Art thou for us, or for our adversaries?" The answer is: "Nay; but as captain of the host of the LORD am I now come." Joshua falls on his face. God is not simply drafted onto Israel's side; Joshua is the one asked to bow. None of these readings makes the chapter easy, and they aren't meant to. Wrestling with a hard text out loud is one honest way to read scripture, and Genesis has a picture of it: Jacob wrestles through the night until daybreak, and comes away blessed, and limping.

Here's the practice: walk in silence. If you can, take this time to walk once around your block, your building or your room, without a word: no phone, no music, no talking. If you can't walk right now, sit, and let your attention walk slowly along the edges of the space you're in. Then bring to mind one hard passage, from the Bible or anywhere, that you'd rather skip. Don't solve it. Don't defend it or dismiss it. Just walk around it, quietly, the way Israel walked around a wall. If you pray, you can bring the hard text to God just as it is. The bell holds the time.
The walls of Jericho. A city circled in silence, a shout, a wall that fell, and a hard chapter that readers wrestle with rather than skip.
Your line: wrestle with hard texts. Today, when you meet a hard passage, a hard headline or a hard conversation, stay with it one minute longer before you look away. Day seven hundred.
